meta.note: All scenarios are fictional composites written for training. Places, people and communities are invented and do not describe any real community. The scenarios are linked to mission contexts by the kind of challenge they involve, not by any claim about a specific population.
meta.scoring: Each choice earns 0–3 points on each of four competencies. A scenario score is points earned divided by points available, per competency.

cq.label: Cultural Intelligence (CQ)
cq.description: CQ stands for Cultural Quotient. Drive, knowledge, strategy and action: being curious about other perspectives, checking your own assumptions and adapting how you behave.

bias.label: Bias Awareness
bias.description: Noticing mental shortcuts such as stereotyping, anchoring and affinity bias, and slowing down when they are likely to shape a decision.

evidence.label: Evidence-Based Decisions
evidence.description: Seeking several independent sources and disaggregated data, and stating uncertainty plainly.

harm.label: Do No Harm & Inclusion
harm.description: Anticipating unintended effects, protecting people at risk and including those most affected, in line with humanitarian principles.

position.label: Social position
position.description: Role, gender, and national, international or uniformed status.
position.ask: How do role, gender and status shape this situation, and who holds power?
examples: Older male leaders vs. the women and girls who collect the water.
A national staff member vs. the team lead.

place.label: Place
place.description: Where the decision happens: a meeting room, a private conversation, a water point, a patrol route or a virtual meeting.
place.ask: Where is this happening, and is that setting safe and reachable for everyone?
examples: The mission meeting vs. the route to the water point.
The meeting room vs. a private conversation afterward.

emotion.label: Emotion / experience
emotion.description: Feeling safe or exposed, heard or overlooked, in that place.
emotion.ask: Who feels safe or exposed here, and who feels heard or overlooked?
examples: Harassment risk on the way to the water point.
Contradicting a supervisor in public can feel disrespectful; raising it privately feels responsible.

voice.label: Voice / power
voice.description: Who speaks, who is missing and whose opinion counts.
voice.ask: Who is speaking, who is missing and whose input is being counted?
examples: Who was consulted, and who was missing from the consultation?
Is input given privately counted or discounted?

biases.name: Affinity bias
biases.definition: Favoring people who seem similar to us in language, education, nationality or manner.
biases.fieldExample: Treating the English-speaking community member as the 'reliable' voice.
biases.counter: Ask whose perspective is missing, and seek it out on purpose.

biases.name: Confirmation bias
biases.definition: Seeking or weighting information that supports what we already believe.
biases.fieldExample: Accepting reports that match the briefing and discounting those that don't.
biases.counter: Before deciding, write down what evidence would change your mind.

biases.name: Anchoring
biases.definition: Relying too heavily on the first piece of information we receive.
biases.fieldExample: A first-day security briefing frames a whole community as hostile for months.
biases.counter: Revisit early assessments on a schedule and compare them with new data.

biases.name: Fundamental attribution error
biases.definition: Explaining others' behavior by character rather than circumstance.
biases.fieldExample: Reading low turnout at a meeting as 'apathy' when the timing clashed with harvest or prayer.
biases.counter: Ask what circumstances could explain the behavior.

biases.name: Stereotyping
biases.definition: Applying a generalization about a group to an individual.
biases.fieldExample: Assuming all young men in an area are linked to an armed group.
biases.counter: Treat cultural knowledge as a hypothesis to test, never as a conclusion about a person.

biases.name: Availability heuristic
biases.definition: Judging how likely or common something is by how easily examples come to mind.
biases.fieldExample: Prioritizing the needs of the district that was in the news.
biases.counter: Use systematic data and note where coverage is thin.

biases.name: Authority and credential bias
biases.definition: Over-weighting views from people with formal titles or international credentials.
biases.fieldExample: Overriding a national colleague's contextual advice in favor of a visiting consultant.
biases.counter: Weigh advice on reasoning and local knowledge, not rank.

biases.name: Savior / paternalism bias
biases.definition: Assuming outsiders know best and communities need rescuing rather than partnership.
biases.fieldExample: Designing a program for a community without consulting it.
biases.counter: Start from local capacities and priorities, and share decision-making.

biases.name: Gender bias
biases.definition: Assumptions about roles, competence or needs based on gender.
biases.fieldExample: Consulting only male leaders on decisions about water points.
biases.counter: Use separate, safe consultation spaces and sex- and age-disaggregated data.

biases.name: Ethnocentrism
biases.definition: Judging other cultures by the norms of your own.
biases.counter: Learn local communication norms from colleagues and suspend judgment.

biases.name: Groupthink
biases.definition: Going along with group consensus to avoid conflict, at the cost of good judgment.
biases.fieldExample: No one questions a team plan because the chief proposed it.
biases.counter: Assign a 'devil's advocate' and invite junior staff to speak first.

biases.name: Deficit framing
biases.definition: Describing people mainly by what they lack rather than by their strengths and agency.
biases.fieldExample: Reports that describe a community only as 'vulnerable' or 'beneficiaries'.
biases.counter: Pair needs with capacities and use people's own descriptions of themselves.

biases.name: Language bias
biases.definition: Equating fluency in a dominant or UN working language with competence or credibility.
biases.fieldExample: Treating halting French as a sign that someone has less expertise.
biases.counter: Provide interpretation and judge the content, not the fluency.

biases.name: Threat bias
biases.definition: Seeing ambiguous behavior as hostile, especially in insecure settings.
biases.fieldExample: Treating a farmer approaching a patrol as a threat by default.
biases.counter: Combine force-protection procedures with de-escalation and local liaison.

frameworks.dimensionsIntro: A person cannot be defined by a single dimension. Building on the Relief Maps+ approach to lived experience (social positions, places and emotions), this tool adds Voice / power for UN fieldwork. Every scenario is tagged with the dimensions it involves, and every response choice records which dimensions it overlooks.
frameworks.dimensionsRule: Each scenario names at least three dimensions in its stem. A dimension is only included when it changes the decision. The dimensions describe the situation; the four competencies score the response.

cqCapabilities.name: CQ Drive
cqCapabilities.question: Am I motivated and confident enough to engage across cultures, even when it is uncomfortable?

cqCapabilities.name: CQ Knowledge
cqCapabilities.question: What do I know, and not know, about the systems, norms and history of this context?

cqCapabilities.name: CQ Strategy
cqCapabilities.question: Am I planning, checking my assumptions and adjusting as I learn?

cqCapabilities.name: CQ Action
cqCapabilities.question: Am I adapting my words, tone and behavior appropriately?

humanitarianPrinciples.name: Humanity
humanitarianPrinciples.text: Human suffering must be addressed wherever it is found.

humanitarianPrinciples.name: Neutrality
humanitarianPrinciples.text: Humanitarian actors must not take sides in hostilities or controversies.

humanitarianPrinciples.name: Impartiality
humanitarianPrinciples.text: Action must be based on need alone, with priority to the most urgent cases and no discrimination.

humanitarianPrinciples.name: Independence
humanitarianPrinciples.text: Humanitarian action must be autonomous from political, economic or military objectives.

pause.name: Pause
pause.text: Notice time pressure and strong feelings. Fast decisions are where bias does the most work.

pause.name: Ask who is missing
pause.text: Whose voices, such as women, youth, minorities, people with disabilities or displaced people, are absent from this decision?

pause.name: Unpack assumptions
pause.text: Name the assumption you are making. Is it about a group, or about this situation?

pause.name: Seek local evidence
pause.text: Check it with national colleagues, community feedback and disaggregated data.

pause.name: Evaluate impact
pause.text: Who might be harmed, excluded or put at risk? Apply Do No Harm and the humanitarian principles.

scenarios.title: Who speaks for the community?
scenarios.summary: Plan a consultation on relocating water points near a protection-of-civilians site.
scenarios.setting: Kalero, a fictional town near a site sheltering displaced families.

steps.prompt: The mission and a water partner must decide where to move two water points that serve the site, and the partner needs an answer within ten days to keep its funding. Your team leader proposes one consultation tomorrow with the five community leaders who usually attend mission meetings, all of them older men, calling them "the community's legitimate voice". The team leader also wants the process kept small, because large gatherings at the site have recently turned tense. What do you recommend?
steps.context: Women and girls collect most of the water. Two incidents of harassment on the path to the current water point were reported last month, and several families with members who have disabilities live at the far edge of the site.

sources.title: IASC Commitments on Accountability to Affected People and PSEA (2017)
IASC Guidelines for Integrating Gender-Based Violence Interventions in Humanitarian Action (2015)

choices.text: Hold the meeting with the five leaders as planned. They are the community's recognized representatives, the partner's deadline is tight and a small meeting keeps tensions down.
choices.feedback: The leaders are the easiest voices to reach, not the most affected ones. A plan agreed only with older men could put the new water points where the people who walk there, mostly women and girls, face the same harassment. A tight deadline is a reason to plan well, not to narrow who is heard.

choices.text: Replace the leaders' meeting with one open meeting for the whole site, announced widely, so that anyone can attend and no single group controls the discussion.
choices.feedback: Opening the door is not the same as hearing everyone. In a large public meeting the same senior men tend to speak first, women and girls may not feel able to contradict them in public, and a big gathering is exactly the setting where tensions have flared.

choices.text: Meet the leaders, and also hold small sessions this week with women, girls and people with disabilities, led by female staff at times and places that suit them.
choices.feedback: This respects existing structures and the deadline while making sure the people most affected are heard safely. Small, separate, well-facilitated sessions are standard practice for accountability to affected people, and they avoid the risks of one large meeting.

choices.text: Skip the leaders, who may act as gatekeepers, and ask women about the options directly at the water point while they wait, so their views are not filtered.
choices.feedback: Centering women is right, but bypassing recognized leaders can trigger a backlash against the women who spoke up. A busy water point is neither private nor safe for talking about harassment, and assuming every leader is a gatekeeper is a stereotype too.

steps.prompt: Only six women come to the first women's session, although more than two hundred households live on the site. Back at the office, a colleague says, "They clearly aren't that interested. The leaders' input should be enough." Your team leader agrees and wants to close the consultation so the partner can start work. Four days remain before the partner's deadline. How do you respond?
steps.context: The session was held at 10:00 on market day, in the mission's community center at the main gate, next to an armed checkpoint. No childcare was offered.

sources.title: IASC Gender Handbook for Humanitarian Action (2017)
IASC Commitments on Accountability to Affected People and PSEA (2017)

choices.text: Agree to close the consultation. The session was announced well in advance, the women had a fair chance to attend and the partner's deadline is real.
choices.feedback: This reads low turnout as lack of interest: the fundamental attribution error. Timing, venue and care duties are far likelier explanations. A market-day session beside an armed checkpoint, with no childcare, screens out most of the women you need to hear.

choices.text: Ask female national staff and women's groups what timing, venue and childcare would work, then rerun the session within four days and update the partner.
choices.feedback: You looked for circumstances before blaming the women, drew on local knowledge and protected the timeline by acting quickly and keeping the partner informed. That is CQ Strategy in practice.

choices.text: Offer a cash payment and a meal to every woman who attends the next session, which should raise attendance quickly without delaying the partner's plan.
choices.feedback: Compensating people for their time can be appropriate where policy allows it, but it treats the symptom. The venue, timing and childcare problems remain, and payments can change who attends and create expectations the mission cannot keep.

choices.text: Send female staff door to door to collect women's views one by one over the next four days, rather than trying a second group session.
choices.feedback: Household visits can reach women who cannot travel, but in four days the team will mostly reach the nearest households, and women may not speak freely with relatives listening. Use visits to complement a well-designed session, not to replace it.

steps.prompt: Forty women attend the rescheduled afternoon session at a women's center inside the site. Several describe harassment by young men on the path to the current water point, and two women privately name one man. The leaders' preferred site for the new points sits on that same path. Your team leader asks you to present "the women's position" at tomorrow's joint meeting with the leaders. What do you do?
steps.context: The women asked that nothing they said be traced back to them. A protection officer and a referral pathway for gender-based violence are available through the protection cluster.

sources.title: IASC Guidelines for Integrating Gender-Based Violence Interventions in Humanitarian Action (2015)
IASC Operational Guidance on Data Responsibility in Humanitarian Action (2023)

choices.text: Present the women's concerns in full at the joint meeting, including the man they named, so that the leaders understand how serious and urgent the situation is.
choices.feedback: Naming the man, or sharing details that point to the women who spoke, breaks the confidentiality they asked for and could expose them to retaliation. Reports of harassment go to protection colleagues through the referral pathway, not to a public meeting.

choices.text: Keep the women's input out of the joint meeting to avoid a confrontation with the leaders, and share it with your team leader later in a private note.
choices.feedback: Avoiding confrontation keeps the meeting calm, but it lets the leaders' preference decide by default. The women were consulted because the location affects their safety. If their input never reaches the decision, the consultation was only for show.

choices.text: Invite three of the women to present their concerns themselves at the joint meeting, so that the leaders hear directly from the people most affected by the decision.
choices.feedback: Hearing directly from women can be powerful, but only if they choose it and are prepared. Asking them to speak in front of the leaders they may be contradicting, on an issue they asked to keep anonymous, can expose them. Offer it as an option, not as the plan.

choices.text: Turn the women's concerns into anonymous safety criteria for any site, such as lighting and routes, and refer the harassment to protection colleagues if they consent.
choices.feedback: Turning the women's input into anonymous, practical criteria puts their safety at the center of the decision without exposing anyone. The harassment itself goes to protection colleagues with the women's consent, which is the survivor-centered route.

takeaways: The easiest voices to reach are not always the most affected.
Low turnout usually reflects barriers such as timing, venue and care duties, not indifference.
Turn sensitive input into anonymous decision criteria, and refer protection concerns through the proper pathway.
debrief.reflection: Think of a recent decision you made. Whose input was easiest to get, and whose did you not hear?

scenarios.title: Lost in translation
scenarios.summary: Assess conflicting accounts of a local dispute that reached you through one interpreter.
scenarios.setting: Drehan, a fictional district where two villages are in a land dispute.

steps.prompt: For three weeks, every interview about the land dispute has gone through Samir, a respected interpreter who grew up in Upper Drehan, one of the two villages. His interpretations consistently support Upper Drehan's account, and your draft report to the head of office, due in five days, already leans that way. A colleague hints that Samir "shades" testimony but gives no examples. Samir has worked with the mission for six years and has received threats for doing so. What do you do?
steps.context: The mission's two other qualified interpreters are fully booked this week. Recordings exist for most of the interviews.

sources.title: OHCHR Manual on Human Rights Monitoring (2011)
UN Guidance for Effective Mediation (2012)

choices.text: Have another interpreter spot-check a sample of recordings, re-interview key sources with someone from neither village and note the sourcing limit, without singling Samir out.
choices.feedback: Spot-checking recordings and diversifying interpreters tests the pattern instead of assuming it either way. Stating the sourcing limit protects the report's impartiality, and treating it as standard practice protects a colleague who already faces risks.

choices.text: Keep working with Samir. He has six years of trusted service, his accounts are consistent across dozens of interviews and a colleague's vague hint is not evidence.
choices.feedback: The hint isn't evidence, but neither is consistency: accounts can agree because they all pass through one channel. Trust in a colleague (affinity) and a draft that already leans one way (confirmation) make it easy to stop checking.

choices.text: Use a different interpreter for the remaining interviews, but keep the draft's conclusions, since three weeks of consistent testimony already gives the report a solid base.
choices.feedback: Changing interpreters from now on helps, but keeping conclusions built entirely on one channel anchors the report on material you haven't checked. Lower Drehan's earlier testimony may need to be heard again.

choices.text: Quietly take Samir off the dispute and set aside every interview he interpreted, so that the final report rests only on material nobody can question.
choices.feedback: This assumes bad faith without evidence, may expose a colleague who already faces threats for working with the UN, and throws away testimony from people who spoke at some risk. Test the pattern before acting on it.

steps.prompt: In a re-interview with a new interpreter, an elder from Lower Drehan speaks at length in indirect, proverb-rich language about "the river that remembers its old bed". Your colleague, short on time, calls the elder "evasive" and suggests leaving the testimony out. The new interpreter will only give a literal translation, saying that explaining the proverbs would mean adding his own opinion. What do you do?
steps.context: Several national staff say this style is a respected way to discuss sensitive matters, such as old boundaries, without naming people. The report is due in two days.

sources.title: OHCHR Manual on Human Rights Monitoring (2011)
UN Values and Behaviours Framework (2021)

choices.text: Leave the testimony out. The report needs clear statements that can be attributed, and including material that nobody can interpret reliably would weaken its credibility.
choices.feedback: Judging one communication style by the norms of another is ethnocentrism. Indirect speech can carry precise meaning, here possibly about where an old boundary ran, and leaving it out silences one village's account.

choices.text: Include the literal translation, and ask the elder to confirm his main point with simple yes-or-no answers at a short follow-up meeting before the deadline.
choices.feedback: Including the testimony is good, but asking an elder to switch to yes-or-no answers can come across as disrespectful and may end the conversation. The meaning is better recovered through cultural interpretation than by demanding a different style.

choices.text: Ask Samir, who knows the local proverbs well, to explain what the elder meant, since he understands the history and language of both villages better than anyone.
choices.feedback: Cultural interpretation is the right instinct, but Samir comes from the other village in the dispute. Asking him to explain Lower Drehan's testimony brings back the very sourcing problem you were correcting.

choices.text: Ask national colleagues from neither village to explain the proverbs in context, and record both the literal and the interpreted meaning, noting who interpreted it.
choices.feedback: This is CQ Knowledge and Strategy: you treat indirectness as meaningful, draw on contextual expertise that isn't tied to either side and keep the report transparent about how the meaning was established.

steps.prompt: Your revised analysis finds that both villages have credible historical claims, and notes that earlier drafts relied on a single interpreter. The head of office, who already briefed a government minister along the lines of your first draft, asks you to "soften the sourcing note" and keep the original conclusion, because changing course "will look like the mission can't make up its mind". What do you do?
steps.context: Both villages will see the mission's public summary. Upper Drehan's leaders have already quoted the head of office's briefing on local radio.

sources.title: UN Guidance for Effective Mediation (2012)
ICSC Standards of Conduct for the International Civil Service (2013)

choices.text: Keep the original conclusion as asked. The head of office is responsible for the mission's relationships, and reversing course in public could damage its credibility.
choices.feedback: Deferring to rank when the evidence has changed is authority bias. Publishing a conclusion you know rests on one channel puts the mission's impartiality at risk with Lower Drehan, which is a bigger credibility problem than a correction.

choices.text: Walk the head of office through the new evidence privately, suggest presenting the update as a fuller picture and keep the sourcing note accurate.
choices.feedback: You respect the hierarchy by raising it privately and offering a way to present the change without embarrassment, but you don't trade accuracy for comfort. Being open about how the evidence improved protects the mission's impartiality.

choices.text: Send your accurate version directly to the mission's senior leadership as well, so that the record is correct whatever the head of office decides to do.
choices.feedback: Accuracy matters, but going over your manager's head before discussing it with them damages trust and turns a question of evidence into a conflict between people. Raise it with the head of office first, and escalate only if needed.

choices.text: Keep the original conclusion in the summary and move the sourcing note to an annex, as a compromise that gives both of you part of what you want.
choices.feedback: An annex few people read doesn't fix a summary both villages will read. Keeping the first conclusion because it came first is anchoring, and Lower Drehan would reasonably see the mission as taking sides.

takeaways: A single information channel produces consistency, not truth.
Indirect speech is not evasiveness. Recover its meaning with help from people tied to neither side.
When the evidence changes, update the analysis and explain why. Accuracy protects impartiality.
debrief.reflection: Which communication styles do you instinctively read as 'credible'? Where did that preference come from?

scenarios.title: Whose expertise counts?
scenarios.summary: A national colleague's warning conflicts with a visiting consultant's recommendation.
scenarios.setting: A fictional mission planning cell preparing a community dialogue initiative.

steps.prompt: An international consultant presents a plan to hold a regional dialogue forum in the provincial capital on the 14th of next month. The deputy head of office has already endorsed it, and invitations go out on Friday. After the meeting, Amani, a national officer with twelve years' experience, tells you quietly that the date falls during mourning observances for a respected local chief, and that the venue, a hotel, belongs to a family linked to one of the factions. What do you do?
steps.context: The consultant presented polished slides in English. Amani is fluent in French and two local languages but rarely speaks in large meetings, which are held in English.

sources.title: UN Values and Behaviours Framework (2021)
UN Guidance for Effective Mediation (2012)

choices.text: Proceed with the endorsed plan. Changing it now would delay the invitations and undercut the deputy head, and the consultant was hired precisely for this expertise.
choices.feedback: An endorsement and a consultancy contract are not evidence. Holding the forum during mourning observances, in a venue tied to one faction, could undermine both attendance and the mission's perceived neutrality.

choices.text: Raise the timing and venue concerns at the next planning meeting yourself, without mentioning Amani, so the change goes through quickly and she isn't put on the spot.
choices.feedback: The decision may improve, but presenting her analysis as your own reinforces the hierarchy that kept Amani quiet. Credit is part of inclusion, and decision-makers should know whose knowledge they rely on. Ask her how she would like to be credited.

choices.text: Ask Amani to present her concerns herself at the next planning meeting, in English, so that leadership hears the warning directly from the person who knows most.
choices.feedback: Giving Amani the floor is well meant, but asking her to present in English, in the large meeting where she rarely speaks, puts the burden on her and keeps the barrier in place. Change the format rather than asking her to fit it.

choices.text: Thank Amani, check the dates and the venue's ownership with other sources, then ask the deputy head to revisit the plan, crediting her as she prefers.
choices.feedback: You weighed the warning on its merits, checked it rather than taking anyone's word for it and gave credit in a way that respects her wishes. That builds a culture where contextual expertise reaches decision-makers.

steps.prompt: The deputy head agrees to move the forum, but the consultant objects in an email to the whole team: "Local sensitivities will always exist. If we accommodate every concern, we will never hold anything." Two senior international colleagues reply in agreement. No national staff respond. You must propose a new date and venue by Thursday. How do you proceed?
steps.context: Last year, a mission event held during an observance in a neighboring province was boycotted by two communities and later described in local media as disrespectful.

sources.title: UN Values and Behaviours Framework (2021)
UN Guidance for Effective Mediation (2012)

choices.text: Reply to all with the evidence from last year's boycott and the media coverage it received, to settle the debate in the email thread before Thursday.
choices.feedback: Evidence helps, but a reply-all debate among senior staff tends to harden positions, and national colleagues who stayed silent in the thread stay silent. The problem is not only the argument but who gets to make it.

choices.text: Go along with the senior colleagues and keep the original date, but add a moment of silence at the forum's opening as a mark of respect.
choices.feedback: Two quick replies from senior colleagues are not a consensus, and a gesture at the opening doesn't fix a date that clashes with mourning. This is groupthink: the silence of national staff is being read as agreement.

choices.text: Hold a short call with national staff and community liaison assistants in French or local languages, and base the new date and venue on their advice.
choices.feedback: You widened who is consulted, lowered the language barrier and based the decision on contextual knowledge rather than on who replied first. Silence in a thread is not agreement, especially when the thread is in a second language.

choices.text: Ask the consultant to choose a new date and venue, since the plan is theirs and they have the most experience organizing forums like this.
choices.feedback: Handing the decision back to the person who missed the issue repeats the original problem. Experience organizing forums is not the same as knowing this province's calendar and alliances.

steps.prompt: The forum goes well, and the deputy head asks you to recommend how planning meetings should run from now on. Meetings are held in English, follow the order of seniority and are dominated by international staff. National officers' contributions usually arrive afterward, by email or in corridor conversations. Some international colleagues worry that changing the format will slow decisions down. What do you recommend?
steps.context: About 70 percent of the planning cell are national staff. Interpretation into French is available on request but has never been requested.

sources.title: UN Values and Behaviours Framework (2021)

choices.text: Share agendas early, accept written input in French or English before meetings, invite national officers to speak first on context items and rotate who facilitates.
choices.feedback: Structural changes reduce language and hierarchy barriers far more than invitations do. Hearing contextual input first also counters anchoring on senior opinions, and written input counts contributions that would otherwise arrive too late.

choices.text: Open each meeting by reminding everyone that all views are welcome, that disagreeing with senior staff is encouraged and that no question is too basic.
choices.feedback: Good intentions are not enough. Without changes to language, speaking order and format, the same people will keep talking, and national officers will keep bringing their points afterward.

choices.text: Provide French interpretation at every meeting from now on and otherwise keep the format, since language is clearly the main barrier for most national officers.
choices.feedback: Interpretation lowers one barrier, but meetings would still follow seniority, so national officers would still speak last, if at all. Language and hierarchy work together here, so fixing one isn't enough.

choices.text: Keep the current format for speed, and formally invite national officers to send their comments in writing after each meeting, as many already do.
choices.feedback: This formalizes the problem. Comments that arrive after decisions are made rarely change them, so national expertise stays outside the room where choices happen.

takeaways: National staff often hold the most important contextual knowledge.
Polished presentations, rank and quick agreement are not evidence.
Inclusion depends on how meetings are structured: language, speaking order and timing.
debrief.reflection: In your last team meeting, who spoke first and longest? Whose views shaped the outcome?

scenarios.title: The data we can reach
scenarios.summary: Prioritize assistance using a needs assessment with significant gaps.
scenarios.setting: A fictional region with an accessible urban center and rural areas that are hard to reach.

steps.prompt: A rapid needs assessment shows the most severe needs in the city's displacement sites. But 80 percent of the interviews were done in areas reachable by road, three rural districts weren't surveyed at all because of flooding, and most respondents were men, because enumerators interviewed heads of household. Leadership wants a one-page summary by tomorrow morning to guide the allocation of a pooled fund. What do you write?
steps.context: Partners report, without data, that some flooded villages may face severe shortages of food and clean water. The fund's allocation window closes in two weeks.

sources.title: Humanitarian principles: General Assembly resolutions 46/182 (1991) and 58/114 (2004)
IASC Gender Handbook for Humanitarian Action (2017)

choices.text: Report that needs are most severe in the city's displacement sites, which is what the data shows, and recommend allocating the fund there while it is open.
choices.feedback: This presents a gap in coverage as a finding. The unsurveyed districts aren't low-need, they're unknown, and a sample of mostly male heads of household may miss needs that women, older people and people with disabilities would report.

choices.text: Report the urban findings, map the coverage and gender gaps, flag partner reports as unverified and recommend a quick remote assessment of rural districts before allocation.
choices.feedback: This is honest about uncertainty and keeps decision-makers from mistaking the absence of data for the absence of need, while giving them a practical next step within the deadline. Impartiality means acting on need, which means finding it.

choices.text: Recommend shifting most of the fund to the flooded rural districts, since several partners on the ground are independently signaling a hidden and growing crisis there.
choices.feedback: This swaps one unverified picture for another. Vivid partner reports are signals worth checking quickly, not evidence on which to move most of a fund away from needs you have measured.

choices.text: Report the findings with a clear, prominent caveat that rural coverage was limited, and leave it to leadership to decide how much weight to give those gaps.
choices.feedback: A caveat is better than silence, but a one-line warning is easy to skip, and it says nothing about who was missing from the sample. Decision-makers need to see the gaps and a way to close them.

steps.prompt: Leadership approves a remote assessment of the flooded districts. With phone networks patchy, a colleague proposes calling the village chiefs whose numbers the mission already has, since they "know everyone's situation". You have five days and no road access. Several villages have no chief on your list, and two are home to a minority group that has been excluded from aid in the past. How do you design the assessment?
steps.context: A women's cooperative and a local health network work in the area and have working radio links. A partner can provide satellite images of the flooding.

sources.title: Humanitarian principles: General Assembly resolutions 46/182 (1991) and 58/114 (2004)
IASC Gender Handbook for Humanitarian Action (2017)

choices.text: Call chiefs, the women's cooperative, health workers and minority-community contacts, check against the satellite images and list the villages you couldn't reach.
choices.feedback: Several independent sources, including those closest to women and to excluded groups, give you a triangulated picture. Recording which villages you couldn't reach keeps the remaining gaps visible instead of quietly closing them.

choices.text: Call the chiefs on your list and ask each of them to report on their neighboring villages as well, so that every village is covered within the five days.
choices.feedback: This gives full coverage on paper, but every answer passes through the same gatekeepers, and the minority villages would be described by neighbors who may have excluded them before. Coverage is not the same as representation.

choices.text: Use the chiefs already on file. They are the recognized local authorities, they can be reached now and the timeline doesn't allow time to build new contact lists.
choices.feedback: The contacts you already have are the easiest to reach, not necessarily the best informed about everyone. Villages without a chief on your list, and the minority group, would simply drop out of the data.

choices.text: Wait until the roads reopen and run a full in-person survey, since data gathered through patchy phone calls won't be reliable enough to act on.
choices.feedback: Remote data has limits, but waiting weeks for better data leaves people without help during the period of greatest risk. Imperfect, triangulated information with its uncertainty stated plainly is usually better than none.

steps.prompt: Your draft report calls the displaced population "helpless beneficiaries" to stress the urgency for donors. A community representative who reviewed it objects: people have organized their own water committees, a school and a savings group, and the report "makes us look like we are waiting to be saved". A donor-relations colleague argues that urgent, emotional language raises more money. How do you revise the report?
steps.context: The representative also points out that the report's photos show only children and older people, and that no one asked permission to use them.

sources.title: UN Principles on Personal Data Protection and Privacy (2018)
IASC Operational Guidance on Data Responsibility in Humanitarian Action (2023)
IASC Commitments on Accountability to Affected People and PSEA (2017)

choices.text: Keep the wording and the photos. The report is written for donors, not for the community, and urgent, emotional language is what gets funding released quickly.
choices.feedback: Deficit framing strips people of agency and tends to produce programs that sideline community structures that already work. Using people's images without consent also breaks basic standards of dignity and data protection, whoever the audience is.

choices.text: Replace "helpless beneficiaries" with "affected people", remove the photos and leave the rest of the report as it is, since the needs analysis itself is sound.
choices.feedback: Neutral wording and removing the photos fix the most visible problems, but the report still describes only needs. Leaving out the committees, the school and the savings group means programs may still be designed for people instead of with them.

choices.text: Describe needs alongside capacities like the committees and the school, use people's own terms for themselves and use only photos people choose and agree to.
choices.feedback: Pairing needs with capacities is more accurate and better for programming, because it points to partners rather than passive recipients. Consent and the community's own terms respect dignity, and donors respond to credible, specific stories too.

choices.text: Write two versions: an urgent, emotional one for donors and a capacity-focused one for the community, so that each audience gets the message that works best for it.
choices.feedback: With two versions, the one that moves resources still portrays people as helpless, and communities usually see donor material eventually. Consistent, accurate framing protects trust as well as dignity.

takeaways: Areas and groups without data are unknown, not low-need.
Triangulate with sources close to women and excluded groups, and keep remaining gaps visible.
Words and images shape programs, so describe capacities as well as needs, with consent.
debrief.reflection: What does your organization's language say about the people it serves?

scenarios.title: When rumors spread
scenarios.summary: Respond to a damaging rumor about the mission circulating on social media.
scenarios.setting: Benza, a fictional city where a rumor claims peacekeepers are protecting an armed group.

steps.prompt: A rumor that peacekeepers secretly protect an armed group is spreading through voice messages and social media, two days after an attack near a mission base killed eleven civilians. A colleague calls it "obviously enemy propaganda that only uneducated people believe" and drafts a strongly worded denial for immediate release in French and English. Community radio hosts tell you people are angry that the attack happened so close to the base. What is your first step?
steps.context: Most residents get their news from local-language radio and voice messages. A youth group has called for a protest outside the base on Friday.

sources.title: UN Global Principles for Information Integrity (2024)
DPO Policy on the Protection of Civilians in UN Peacekeeping (2023)

choices.text: Approve the denial for immediate release. Speed matters with disinformation, and every hour a false claim goes unanswered lets it harden into accepted fact.
choices.feedback: Speed matters, but writing believers off as "uneducated" misreads a real grievance. A sharp denial in languages most residents don't use, two days after civilians died near the base, can sound indifferent and deepen distrust.

choices.text: Say nothing publicly for now. Any response gives the rumor more oxygen, and it will probably fade once people's attention moves on to other news.
choices.feedback: Not amplifying a rumor can be wise, but silence while people grieve and feel unprotected reads as indifference. With a protest planned for Friday, others will fill the gap.

choices.text: Listen first: meet radio hosts, youth, women's and faith groups today, then respond in local languages with verifiable facts and candor about the mandate's limits.
choices.feedback: Rumors often carry real fears and unmet expectations. Understanding the grievance first, then responding through trusted channels, in local languages and honestly about what the mission can and cannot do, builds more trust than a denial alone.

choices.text: Ask the mission's analysts to trace who started the rumor, then publish evidence of the coordinated campaign behind it, so that its source is publicly discredited.
choices.feedback: Knowing whether a campaign is coordinated is useful, but leading with it assumes the rumor is pure propaganda and ignores why it resonates with ordinary residents. Publicly naming sources can also put people at risk and draw the mission into the conflict.

steps.prompt: The listening sessions reveal that the attack happened while the base's quick reaction force was deployed elsewhere, and that a community alert about the armed group reached the mission six hours before the attack but was not acted on. Leadership is preparing a town hall for Friday, the day of the planned protest. Your director wants the town hall to "focus on the positive" and leave out the late alert. How do you advise?
steps.context: An internal review of how the alert was handled has begun. The residents who sent the alert have already told radio hosts about it.

sources.title: DPO Policy on the Protection of Civilians in UN Peacekeeping (2023)

choices.text: Follow the director's line. With an internal review under way, discussing the alert in public could prejudge its findings and expose the mission to legal risk.
choices.feedback: The review is a real constraint, but residents already know about the alert. Leaving it out will look like a cover-up and confirm the rumor's core claim: that the mission doesn't act on what it knows.

choices.text: Acknowledge the late alert in full, including which units failed to act and why, so that residents can see the mission is hiding nothing.
choices.feedback: Candor is right, but naming units and assigning blame before the review concludes can be unfair to personnel, compromise the review and inflame tensions on the day of a protest. Acknowledge the facts and the process without prejudging the outcome.

choices.text: Postpone the town hall until after the protest and the review, so that the mission can give residents complete answers instead of partial ones.
choices.feedback: Complete answers matter, but postponing tells residents the mission is avoiding the people it is meant to protect, just when their anger is highest. Honest, partial engagement now usually beats complete answers too late.

choices.text: Advise acknowledging the late alert and the review now, committing to share the findings, and explaining what is changing in how alerts are handled.
choices.feedback: This is candid without prejudging the review. It names what residents already know and shows accountability through a concrete process and concrete changes. Credibility comes from admitting gaps, not avoiding them.

steps.prompt: The town hall will go ahead. Your director proposes a panel of the head of office, a representative of the force commander and the police commissioner, with questions submitted in writing in advance "to keep it orderly". Radio hosts warn that people want to speak directly, and that young men from the neighborhood near the attack feel they are always treated as suspects. Who should be on the panel, and how should it run?
steps.context: The venue is a school hall that holds 300 people. Women's groups say many women will not attend an evening event.

sources.title: DPO Policy on the Protection of Civilians in UN Peacekeeping (2023)
UN Global Principles for Information Integrity (2024)

choices.text: Pair mission leaders with youth, women's and faith representatives, hold an afternoon session with open questions in local languages and publish follow-up commitments.
choices.feedback: Sharing the platform with trusted local voices, taking open questions and choosing a time that works for women show respect and accountability. Published commitments give residents a way to hold the mission to its word.

choices.text: Keep the senior mission panel, to show that leadership takes the attack seriously, but take questions from the floor as well as the written ones.
choices.feedback: Open questions help, but a panel of senior mission officials only reinforces the distance that feeds rumors. Trusted local voices on the panel make the conversation two-way.

choices.text: Keep the director's format, and ask the security section to screen attendees at the door, paying particular attention to young men from the area of the attack.
choices.feedback: Security planning is legitimate, but singling out young men from one neighborhood treats a whole group as suspects, the very grievance they raised. It would likely turn the town hall into fresh evidence for the rumor.

choices.text: Invite local youth and women's leaders to join the senior panel, but keep the evening time and the written questions, to limit the risk of disruption on the day.
choices.feedback: A shared panel is a real improvement, but an evening event many women won't attend, and pre-screened written questions, limit who is heard. Who is on stage matters, and so does who can reach the room and speak in it.

takeaways: Behind a rumor there is often a real grievance, so listen before you respond.
Be candid about known failures and about the process for addressing them.
Messengers, language, timing and format decide who is heard.
debrief.reflection: When people believe something you know is false, what explanations do you reach for first?

scenarios.title: An invitation to dinner
scenarios.summary: Balance local hospitality norms with UN standards of conduct.
scenarios.setting: A fictional capital where you are meeting a regional organization's delegation for the first time.

steps.prompt: After a productive first meeting with a regional organization's delegation, your counterpart, a senior official, warmly invites you to a family dinner at her home on Saturday and presents a handcrafted brass lamp made in her home town. Your office expects to sign a cooperation agreement with her organization next month. A colleague whispers, "Refuse both, now. It's the rules." How do you respond in the moment?
steps.context: Here, declining hospitality outright can be read as rejecting the relationship. UN staff may not accept gifts from governments, or from other sources without approval, but an unexpected gift that can't be refused without embarrassment can be accepted on behalf of the Organization, then reported and handed over.

sources.title: UN Staff Regulation 1.2 (j)–(l) on gifts: UN Ethics Office fact sheet
ICSC Standards of Conduct for the International Civil Service (2013)

choices.text: Decline both on the spot, politely but clearly, explaining that UN rules forbid staff from accepting any gifts or private invitations from partner organizations.
choices.feedback: Integrity matters, but refusing both on the spot can feel like rejecting the relationship, however politely it is done. The rules are also more nuanced than a flat ban: some gifts can be accepted on behalf of the Organization, and hospitality depends on the circumstances.

choices.text: Thank her warmly, accept the lamp on behalf of the Organization, to be reported and handed over, and say you'd be honored to come once you've checked with your office.
choices.feedback: This honors the gesture while staying within the rules. The lamp goes to the Organization, not to you, and is reported and handed over, and you don't commit to a private dinner before checking it against next month's agreement. The Ethics Office can advise on the invitation.

choices.text: Accept both personally and without fuss. Refusing a gift here would be seen as culturally insensitive, and she clearly expects you to take it home.
choices.feedback: Cultural sensitivity never overrides integrity obligations, least of all a month before an agreement with her organization. Assuming she expects you to bend your rules also stereotypes a senior official who probably knows UN rules well.

choices.text: Accept the lamp and the dinner invitation graciously now, then report both to your office first thing on Monday and follow whatever it decides.
choices.feedback: Reporting is right, but the lamp should be accepted for the Organization and reported straight away, not kept until Monday, and you would have committed to private hospitality from a counterpart a month before an agreement. If your office then says no, withdrawing is more awkward than a warm, conditional answer now.

steps.prompt: You check with the Ethics Office, inform your supervisor and go to the dinner. At the dinner, your counterpart's brother mentions that his consulting firm plans to bid on a UN contract your office will evaluate, and asks whether you could "put in a good word". The family is warm and attentive, and other guests are listening. How do you respond?
steps.context: You sit on the evaluation panel for that contract. Refusing sharply in front of the guests would embarrass your hosts.

sources.title: UN Staff Regulation 1.2 (m) on conflicts of interest: UN Ethics Office fact sheet

choices.text: Promise to mention his firm to colleagues. It costs nothing, keeps a warm evening pleasant, and you will still evaluate his bid on its merits like any other.
choices.feedback: Even a small promise creates a conflict of interest, and the warmth of the evening is exactly how affinity bias works. You sit on the panel, so a "good word" is not yours to give.

choices.text: Tell him firmly, in front of the guests, that his request is inappropriate and that you will have to report it to the UN tomorrow.
choices.feedback: Your boundary is right, but a public rebuke embarrasses your hosts in their own home and turns a manageable moment into a confrontation. You can be firm without being harsh, and handle reporting through the proper channel.

choices.text: Explain kindly that you can't discuss a tender, point him to the open procurement process, change the subject and disclose the approach to your head of office.
choices.feedback: You protected the process without humiliating anyone: a kind, clear boundary, a pointer to the fair route open to every bidder and prompt disclosure. A possible conflict of interest must be disclosed to your head of office so it can be managed, here probably by your stepping back from the evaluation.

choices.text: Smile, avoid answering and steer the conversation elsewhere, then put the exchange behind you, since nothing was promised and no harm was done.
choices.feedback: Deflecting gracefully keeps the evening pleasant, but saying nothing afterward leaves a possible conflict of interest undisclosed. Staff must disclose actual and possible conflicts to their head of office, even when nothing was promised.

steps.prompt: You disclose the conversation and step back from the evaluation panel. At the next team meeting, a colleague comments, "That's just how business works in this region. Everyone is somebody's cousin. We should stop accepting invitations from partners altogether." Two colleagues nod. Your supervisor asks what the office should learn from the episode. What do you suggest?
steps.context: The office works with partners from many countries in the region, and several team members are from the region. Your counterpart was not involved in her brother's request.

sources.title: UN Staff Regulation 1.2 (m) on conflicts of interest: UN Ethics Office fact sheet
UN Values and Behaviours Framework (2021)

choices.text: Agree that partners here often mix family and business, and propose a simple blanket policy of declining all hospitality from partners anywhere in the region.
choices.feedback: One person's request is not a regional trait. A blanket ban built on a stereotype would insult partners who follow the rules, including your counterpart, and damage relationships the office depends on.

choices.text: Let the comment pass to avoid tension in the meeting, and suggest that the office reissue the UN guidance on gifts and hospitality to all staff.
choices.feedback: Refreshing the guidance is useful, but letting the generalization pass signals that it's acceptable, including to colleagues from the region who heard it. Address the comment calmly, then fix the process.

choices.text: Point out that your counterpart wasn't involved in the request, and suggest the office carry on as before, since the rules clearly worked as intended this time.
choices.feedback: Defending your counterpart is fair, but "the rules worked" depended on you handling a private dinner well. The office can learn something practical, so that the next colleague in that situation isn't improvising.

choices.text: Say calmly that one person's request says nothing about a region, and propose clear hospitality guidance, routine disclosure of approaches and briefings for new staff.
choices.feedback: You challenged the generalization without shaming anyone and turned the episode into practical learning. Clear guidance and routine disclosure protect staff and partners alike, without treating a whole region as a risk.

takeaways: You can follow the rules and still respect the relationship.
Disclose approaches early, and step back from decisions where you have a conflict of interest.
One person's behavior is not a cultural trait. Fix processes, not reputations.
debrief.reflection: How would you explain a UN rule warmly, in a way that strengthens the relationship?

scenarios.title: Carrying history
scenarios.summary: Engage a community whose past experience of international presences has eroded trust.
scenarios.setting: A fictional neighborhood whose residents remember past harms linked to international actors.

steps.prompt: At your first community meeting in the neighborhood, an older resident stands and lists harms that people here link to international actors over the years: a disease outbreak, cases of sexual exploitation and abuse, and promised jobs that never came. "Why should we trust you?" he asks. The room goes quiet. Your supervisor, sitting beside you, whispers that you should move on to the project briefing. What do you say?
steps.context: The UN has publicly apologized for its role in some past harms in contexts like this one. Several people in the room have direct experience of them.

sources.title: UN News: the Secretary-General apologizes to the people of Haiti (2016)
IASC Commitments on Accountability to Affected People and PSEA (2017)

choices.text: Acknowledge the harms and the anger without defensiveness, explain the reporting channels that exist now and ask what residents would need to see to rebuild trust.
choices.feedback: Acknowledging the history, pointing to concrete accountability channels and asking what trust would look like treats residents as partners. It also respects the courage it took to speak first.

choices.text: Explain respectfully that this office has a different mandate and different staff, so the past is not a fair basis for judging the current project or its team.
choices.feedback: To the community it is one institution, and people who were harmed don't experience mandates as separate. Distancing yourself from the history dismisses real experience and confirms the distrust.

choices.text: Promise warmly that things will be different this time, and say you will personally make sure that residents see real, lasting benefits from this new project.
choices.feedback: The intent is good, but promises you can't personally guarantee deepen distrust when they aren't kept, especially where broken promises are part of the history. Commit to specific, verifiable actions instead.

choices.text: Thank him for speaking, assure him that his concerns will be passed to the right office and continue with the project briefing, as your supervisor suggests.
choices.feedback: Passing the concern on is something, but moving straight on tells the room that its history is a distraction from your agenda. A few minutes of real acknowledgment now will shape how everything after it is heard.

steps.prompt: After the meeting, the same resident takes you aside. He says a staff member of a partner organization offered his granddaughter a job in exchange for "a relationship". The family doesn't want to give its name, fears losing its food assistance and asks you not to tell anyone in the neighborhood. Your partner focal point says he knows the staff member and "can sort it out quietly". What do you do?
steps.context: All UN personnel must report suspected sexual exploitation and abuse through designated channels, and so must the humanitarian partners the UN works with. The safety, consent and confidentiality of the person harmed guide what follows.

sources.title: ST/SGB/2003/13: Special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and sexual abuse
IASC Six Core Principles Relating to Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (2019)
UN: How to report sexual exploitation and abuse

choices.text: Let the partner focal point handle it quietly. He knows the staff member, it respects the family's wish for discretion, and a formal report could cost the family its assistance.
choices.feedback: An informal fix by someone who knows the accused protects the accused, not his granddaughter. Suspected sexual exploitation and abuse must be reported through designated channels, and aid must never depend on anyone staying silent.

choices.text: Reassure him that reporting won't affect the family's aid, explain the confidential support open to his granddaughter and report via the PSEA channel, sharing only what's needed.
choices.feedback: You corrected the fear that keeps people silent (aid is free, and reporting never affects it), offered support that depends on his granddaughter's consent and met your obligation to report through the designated channel for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA), sharing as little identifying detail as possible. Investigating is for specialists, not for you or the partner.

choices.text: Write down his full account, including names, and file a formal complaint right away, even though he asked you not to, because protecting his granddaughter comes first.
choices.feedback: Reporting is required, but taking over his account without explaining what happens next, or collecting more identifying detail than needed, can expose the family and break trust. Report what's needed, and keep the family informed and in control of its own involvement.

choices.text: Promise to keep it confidential, as he asks, and give him the PSEA hotline number so that the family can report it themselves if they decide to.
choices.feedback: Respecting the family's wishes matters, but as UN personnel you have your own obligation to report suspected sexual exploitation, and the power gap between an aid worker and a family that depends on aid is exactly why. Their consent guides support and their own involvement, not whether the concern is reported.

steps.prompt: Months later, residents ask for a simple way to raise concerns about any UN or partner personnel. The current system is an email address and a hotline answered in English and French during office hours. Many residents speak only the local language, few have reliable internet, and women say they can't call from home without being overheard. Headquarters offers to fund a reporting app. What do you propose?
steps.context: A network of community groups, including women's associations and faith groups, already meets weekly across the neighborhood.

sources.title: IASC Best Practice Guide on Inter-Agency Community-Based Complaint Mechanisms (2016)
IASC Commitments on Accountability to Affected People and PSEA (2017)

choices.text: Build the app, with reporting in the local language. It would be confidential, available around the clock, cheap to run and easy for headquarters to monitor.
choices.feedback: An app helps some residents, but it reaches those with smartphones, data and literacy, not the women who can't call from home or the people without reliable internet. Channels must work for the people least able to use them.

choices.text: Keep the email address and hotline, and run a strong awareness campaign on radio and posters so that residents know these channels exist and how to use them.
choices.feedback: Awareness doesn't remove the barriers residents described: language, internet access and being overheard at home. A channel people know about but can't safely use doesn't work.

choices.text: Design channels with residents: focal points in existing groups, local-language reporting, safe in-person options for women and clear rules on data protection.
choices.feedback: Community-based complaint channels designed with residents, in their language and with safe options for women, are central to accountability to affected people. Clear rules on how information is protected are what make people willing to use them.

choices.text: Put locked complaint boxes in busy public places around the neighborhood, with simple forms in the local language, emptied every week by mission staff.
choices.feedback: Local-language forms help, but a box in a public place means being seen using it, and written forms exclude people who can't write. Boxes can be one channel among several, placed where people can use them discreetly.

takeaways: Communities experience the UN as one institution.
Acknowledgment and specific, verifiable actions do more than reassurance.
Report suspected sexual exploitation and abuse through designated channels, with the survivor's safety and choices at the center.
Design complaint channels with residents, for the people least able to use them.
debrief.reflection: How do you respond when people direct anger at you for things you didn't personally do?

scenarios.title: Beyond the label
scenarios.summary: Design a reintegration dialogue that includes former combatants and host communities.
scenarios.setting: A fictional rural municipality with former combatants, host farmers and Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities.

steps.prompt: You are helping design a dialogue between people in the reintegration process and the host community about a shared farming project. The municipal official says host families "will never sit with ex-combatants" and proposes keeping the groups in separate meetings permanently. Last month, a meeting in a neighboring municipality ended in shouting, and the official doesn't want a repeat before local elections in three months. What do you do?
steps.context: Some host community members want dialogue, especially about land and roads. Others fear stigma or reprisals. Indigenous and Afro-descendant authorities have their own decision-making structures and have not yet been consulted.

sources.title: UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007), article 18
UN Guidance for Effective Mediation (2012)

choices.text: Accept the official's assessment. Officials know their community, the election period is sensitive and pushing for joint meetings could cause exactly the incident everyone fears.
choices.feedback: A sweeping claim about a whole group is a hypothesis, not a fact, and some host families want dialogue. Permanent separation would entrench stigma and leave the decision to the person most worried about the election, not to the communities.

choices.text: Organize a joint meeting next week anyway, with experienced facilitators and security in place, to show the official and the community that reconciliation is possible.
choices.feedback: Testing the assumption is right, but forcing a timeline puts the mission's goals ahead of participants' safety and readiness, especially after last month's incident. Readiness has to come from the participants.

choices.text: Hold separate meetings for now, and plan joint activities for after the elections, once the official agrees that the political climate is calmer and safer.
choices.feedback: Phasing is sensible, but this lets one official set the agenda and leaves out the ethnic authorities and the host families who want dialogue now. The communities' readiness, not the electoral calendar, should set the pace.

choices.text: Consult each group safely and separately, including Indigenous and Afro-descendant authorities and women's groups, then build joint activities at a pace they agree to.
choices.feedback: Phased, consent-based approaches respect safety concerns and test the official's assumption instead of accepting or overriding it. Consulting ethnic authorities through their own structures respects their right to take part in decisions that affect them, which for Indigenous peoples is set out in UNDRIP article 18.

steps.prompt: In the separate consultations, women in the reintegration process say the planned meeting times clash with childcare, and that a few male former commanders dominate decisions in their cooperative. A women's group from the host community says it would join a project on seeds and water if it isn't "run by the same men". A colleague suggests handling the women's issues later, "once the main dialogue is working". What do you do?
steps.context: The peace agreement in this fictional context commits to a gender perspective in reintegration. The cooperative's board is elected by its members.

sources.title: IDDRS module 5.10: Women, Gender and DDR
Security Council resolution 1325 (2000) on women, peace and security

choices.text: Design for women from the start: workable times, childcare, a joint women's group on seeds and water and support for women running for the board.
choices.feedback: Gender is part of the design, not an add-on. Practical arrangements, a space the women asked for and support for leadership under the cooperative's own rules address both the barriers and the imbalance of power.

choices.text: Agree to deal with the women's issues later. The main dialogue is still fragile, and adding new demands at this stage could overload it before it has started.
choices.feedback: "Later" usually means never, and a dialogue built around a few male former commanders will reproduce their dominance. Women's participation is part of what makes the dialogue work, not a burden on it.

choices.text: Ask the former commanders who run the cooperative to make room for women, since they hold the authority there and can make it happen quickly.
choices.feedback: Engaging the cooperative's leaders matters, but asking them to "make room" keeps women's participation dependent on their goodwill. Women need their own voice in the process and a real route to leadership under the cooperative's rules.

choices.text: Create a separate project for women only, with its own funding, so they can take part without having to deal with the cooperative at all.
choices.feedback: A women-only space can be valuable, but on its own it leaves the cooperative, with its land, money and decisions, in the hands of the same few men. Combine safe spaces with a real share of power in the main structure.

steps.prompt: The joint project is about to launch. Your draft materials, a poster and a radio spot, describe participants only as "ex-combatants", and the poster shows a photo of men in uniform at the disarmament ceremony. A host farmer warns that the poster could make participants targets for armed groups still active nearby. The communications office says "ex-combatant" is the technical term used in the mandate. What do you change?
steps.context: Many participants are now farmers, parents and cooperative members. Several were recruited as children.

sources.title: Paris Principles on children associated with armed forces or armed groups (2007)
UN Principles on Personal Data Protection and Privacy (2018)

choices.text: Keep the term and the photo. They are accurate, they match the mandate, and changing them could look as if the mission is hiding who the project is for.
choices.feedback: Technical terms belong in mandates, but in public materials they fix people in their past, and here they could expose participants to armed groups. Accuracy includes who people are now.

choices.text: Use person-first language that reflects participants' current roles, check it with them, drop identifying images and review security risks with the protection team.
choices.feedback: Asking people how they want to be described respects their agency, and removing identifying images addresses a real security risk. Labels can fix people in their past. Good materials show who they are now.

choices.text: Replace "ex-combatants" with "people in the reintegration process", but keep the ceremony photo, which shows the history the project builds on and celebrates.
choices.feedback: Better wording helps, but the photo still identifies individuals while armed groups remain active nearby, and no one asked participants how they want to be shown. Safety and consent come before storytelling.

choices.text: Remove any mention of reintegration from the materials and present the project simply as a general farming initiative for the whole municipality.
choices.feedback: Avoiding labels can reduce stigma, but hiding the project's purpose can backfire when people find out, and it decides for participants how visible they want to be. Ask them, and design the materials with them.

takeaways: Claims about whole groups are hypotheses to test.
Build participation in phases, with consent, and make gender part of the main design.
Labels and images shape identity and safety, so ask people how they want to be described.
debrief.reflection: Which labels do you use at work that the people described might not choose for themselves?

scenarios.title: What's in a name?
scenarios.summary: Handle contested place names and terminology impartially.
scenarios.setting: A fictional area where communities use different names for the same towns.

steps.prompt: Your draft weekly situation report uses the place names favored by the community you work with most, the names you learned on your first posting here. A national colleague from the other community notices and says quietly that people there will read the report as the mission taking sides. The report goes to headquarters and partners in two hours, and your supervisor has already cleared it. What do you do?
steps.context: The mission has terminology guidance for this area. You haven't looked at it since your induction.

sources.title: ICSC Standards of Conduct for the International Civil Service (2013)
UN map disclaimer: names and designations do not imply UN endorsement

choices.text: Keep the names for now, since the report is already cleared and the deadline is close, and look into the terminology question properly next week with your supervisor.
choices.feedback: Familiar terms feel neutral to you because you learned them first, which is anchoring. Sent to headquarters and partners, they can signal partiality, and the fix is quick now and much harder once the report is out.

choices.text: Switch to the other community's names throughout, so that the report reflects your colleague's concern and reassures that community before it goes out.
choices.feedback: This responds quickly, but it just moves the bias to the other side. The mission's guidance exists so that its reporting uses agreed terms that neither community owns.

choices.text: Check the mission's terminology guidance, apply the approved terms consistently, tell your supervisor about the change before the report goes out and thank your colleague.
choices.feedback: Approved terminology protects impartiality, and telling your supervisor keeps the clearance honest. Thanking your colleague encourages people to raise issues like this, especially those who raise them quietly.

choices.text: Use both communities' names side by side, separated by a slash, wherever a contested place appears, to show clearly that the mission takes no side.
choices.feedback: Dual names can be a fair solution, and some missions use them, but improvising your own convention is risky: the order of the names, and which places get two, can still signal a side. Check what the mission's guidance says first.

steps.prompt: A week later, a community leader you trust sends you a long, emotional message about an incident at a checkpoint, using a loaded term for the other community's security forces. Your supervisor wants the incident in today's report and suggests quoting the message directly "to show the community's perspective". You haven't heard from the other community or from the mission's military observers. How do you report it?
steps.context: The mission's guidance asks reports to attribute claims clearly and to avoid adopting either party's terminology in the mission's own voice.

sources.title: OHCHR Manual on Human Rights Monitoring (2011)

choices.text: Quote the leader's message in full as the main account of the incident, since this leader has always been reliable and the community's perspective deserves to be heard.
choices.feedback: Trust in a source is affinity, not verification. Leading with one party's account, in its own loaded terms, makes the mission's report sound like that community's statement.

choices.text: Leave the incident out of today's report until the other community and the military observers have confirmed what actually happened at the checkpoint.
choices.feedback: Caution is understandable, but leaving out a reported incident can delay the response to a real protection concern, and the community that raised it will notice. You can report early if you report carefully: attributed and marked as unverified.

choices.text: Paraphrase the leader's account in neutral language, without attribution, and present it as the mission's own description of what happened at the checkpoint.
choices.feedback: Neutral wording is right, but without attribution the report presents one party's unverified account as the mission's own finding. Readers need to know who said what and what has been confirmed.

choices.text: Report it as an unverified allegation from community sources, in neutral terms, note that other accounts are being sought and update when the observers report.
choices.feedback: Clear attribution and neutral wording let you report promptly without adopting either party's language or conclusions. Saying what is still being verified is accurate and protects the mission's impartiality.

steps.prompt: The mission is preparing a public map of services for both communities. Under time pressure, the design team used one community's place names, because those are the names in the open mapping data they downloaded. A youth group from the other community has already posted a screenshot of the draft, calling it "proof" that the UN is biased. Your supervisor asks you to handle it. What do you do?
steps.context: Residents of both communities use the services on the map. The approved terminology list covers most, but not all, of the places shown.

sources.title: UN map disclaimer: names and designations do not imply UN endorsement
UN Global Principles for Information Integrity (2024)

choices.text: Correct the map to the approved terms, agree names for the missing places with colleagues from both communities and explain the change publicly and factually.
choices.feedback: You fixed the source of the problem, filled the gaps with input from both sides rather than one, and answered the public concern openly instead of with silence or defensiveness.

choices.text: Keep the map as it is, since the names come from a widely used open dataset, and explain to the youth group that the mission didn't choose them.
choices.feedback: A dataset isn't neutral just because it is widely used: its names reflect whoever contributed them. Once they appear on a UN map, they are the mission's choice, whatever the source.

choices.text: Quietly correct the map to the approved terms and republish it without commenting on the screenshot, to avoid drawing even more attention to the youth group's post.
choices.feedback: Correcting the map is the key step, but staying silent leaves the "proof" claim unanswered, and a quiet change can look like an attempt to hide a mistake. A short, factual explanation builds more trust.

choices.text: Withdraw the map entirely until a full terminology review has been completed, so that the mission isn't seen to publish anything contested again.
choices.feedback: Withdrawing avoids controversy, but residents of both communities lose information about services they need, possibly for weeks. Correct what you can now with approved terms, and fill the gaps carefully.

takeaways: Terminology can signal partiality, even when it feels neutral to you.
Attribute claims, mark what is unverified and never adopt a party's terms in the mission's own voice.
Fix mistakes openly. Silence and withdrawal can also look like taking sides.
debrief.reflection: Which words in your field have politically contested meanings?

scenarios.title: The approaching farmer
scenarios.summary: Make a split-second judgment during a patrol near agricultural land.
scenarios.setting: Farmland near a fictional village during the harvest season.

steps.prompt: Your patrol is moving slowly along a farm track at harvest time. A man in his twenties runs toward the lead vehicle from a field, waving both arms and shouting in a language no one in the vehicle speaks.
