The morning briefing warned of "tensions with young men in the area", and a member of your patrol raises a weapon and shouts at him to stop. He keeps coming, pointing at the track ahead. What do you do?
steps.context: Your language assistant is in the second vehicle, about 30 meters behind. UN guidelines require any use of force to respect gradation, necessity and proportionality, and every reasonable effort to resolve a confrontation by other means.

sources.title: Guidelines on the Use of Force by Military Components in UN Peacekeeping Operations (2017)
DPO Policy on the Protection of Civilians in UN Peacekeeping (2023)

choices.text: Back up the soldier: order the man to stop and lie on the ground, and keep weapons on him until he complies, since the briefing flagged young men as a risk.
choices.feedback: The briefing anchored a group stereotype onto one person. Escalating with weapons against someone who may be trying to help could injure a civilian, and it would confirm every fear the village has about the mission.

choices.text: Halt, have the weapon lowered while the patrol stays alert, show open hands and bring the language assistant forward to find out what he needs.
choices.feedback: Force protection and de-escalation go together: the patrol stays ready while you lower the temperature and get information. Pointing at the track ahead could be a warning. Information comes before interpretation.

choices.text: Drive on past him carefully to avoid a confrontation, and report the encounter to the operations room so that it can be followed up later by others.
choices.feedback: Avoiding a confrontation is sensible, but driving on ignores what he may be trying to tell you, and he is pointing at the track you are about to use. Missing urgent information can be as dangerous as escalating.

choices.text: Step out alone to meet him halfway, taking off your helmet, to show trust and make clear that the mission is there to protect civilians.
choices.feedback: Showing trust is the right instinct, but abandoning force-protection procedures puts you at risk, and the field or the track ahead may be dangerous. Without the language assistant, you still won't understand what he is saying.

steps.prompt: Through the language assistant, the man explains that he found a metal object, which he thinks is a shell, half-buried in the track 200 meters ahead, on the route children take to the fields. He is shaken and angry that he was threatened. Villagers are gathering. The patrol is already late for a meeting with the village council, and your sergeant suggests pushing the object off the track with a vehicle so you can continue. What do you do?
steps.context: Mission procedure: no one touches or moves the object, everyone keeps clear, and it is reported through the chain of command to the explosive ordnance disposal team, the nearest of which is two hours away.

sources.title: IMAS 12.10: Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (2020)
DPO Policy on the Protection of Civilians in UN Peacekeeping (2023)

choices.text: Have a vehicle push the object to the side of the track, so it's out of the children's way and the patrol can reach the council meeting on time.
choices.feedback: Moving explosive ordnance is extremely dangerous and is a task for trained specialists only. Doing it to keep to a schedule risks lives, including those of the villagers now gathering nearby.

choices.text: Cordon off the area, report it to the disposal team and continue to the council meeting with most of the patrol, leaving two soldiers behind at the cordon.
choices.feedback: The safety steps are right, but rushing off without acknowledging the man who was threatened, or explaining to the villagers what is happening, misses a moment that will shape how the village sees the mission.

choices.text: Keep everyone back, report the object up the chain of command, warn villagers to keep children away and thank the man, acknowledging he was wrongly threatened.
choices.feedback: You followed the ordnance procedure, protected civilians and acknowledged the harm done by the earlier reaction. The council will understand a delay for this, if you tell them why. Respect and safety reinforce each other here.

choices.text: Keep everyone clear and report the object, but hold the man for questioning until the disposal team confirms that he had nothing to do with placing it there.
choices.feedback: The safety steps are right, but treating the person who warned you as a suspect, without any evidence, is threat bias again. It punishes the behavior you most want to encourage: civilians reporting dangers to the mission.

steps.prompt: The object was an unexploded mortar round, and the disposal team destroys it safely. That evening, you prepare the patrol report and the team debrief. Two soldiers are embarrassed about raising a weapon and would prefer the first minutes not be mentioned. The intelligence officer who wrote the morning briefing asks you to describe the man as a "military-age male" in the report. How do you handle the report and the debrief?
steps.context: The village council has asked for a meeting about the incident. Children use several tracks in the area during the harvest.

sources.title: Guidelines on the Use of Force by Military Components in UN Peacekeeping Operations (2017)
DPO Policy on the Protection of Civilians in UN Peacekeeping (2023)

choices.text: Use the intelligence officer's wording and leave out the first minutes. Both are common practice, and dwelling on a mistake that caused no harm would only hurt morale.
choices.feedback: Describing a civilian who helped you as a "military-age male" carries the briefing's threat framing into the record, and leaving out the escalation hides the most important lesson. Debriefs exist so that near-misses don't happen again.

choices.text: Record the facts accurately, including the escalation, but keep the debrief short and focused on the ordnance procedure, to spare the two soldiers further embarrassment.
choices.feedback: An accurate report matters, but a debrief that skips the first minutes misses why the team reacted as it did. Discussing it without blame is how the whole team learns, not just the two soldiers.

choices.text: Report accurately and hold a blame-free debrief, but decline the council's meeting request for now, since the incident is still being reported up the chain of command.
choices.feedback: The report and debrief are right, but declining the council leaves the village's questions unanswered after a frightening incident. Meeting soon builds trust and a chance to agree on how villagers can safely report dangers.

choices.text: Describe him as a civilian who reported ordnance, record the escalation, debrief without blame on how the briefing shaped reactions and meet the village council.
choices.feedback: Accurate, neutral language, an honest record and a blame-free debrief turn one incident into learning for the whole team. Meeting the council closes the loop with the community, and it is worth raising with the briefing's author how group-level warnings are worded.

takeaways: Briefings can prime threat bias, so separate group trends from individual behavior.
De-escalation and force protection go together, and civilians who warn you deserve thanks, not suspicion.
Record and debrief your reactions as well as your actions, in neutral language.
debrief.reflection: How do your briefings describe local populations, and what might that prime you to see?

scenarios.title: Who gets heard, and how?
scenarios.summary: A colleague raises a problem privately instead of in the meeting. Respond as the team lead.
scenarios.setting: A coordination meeting at a field office in Sarel, a fictional city. Maya is a fictional colleague; her preference for raising concerns privately is personal, not a cultural label for any group.

steps.prompt: In a coordination meeting, you present a new distribution schedule that has already been shared in draft with partners. Maya, a national staff member, notices that it overlaps with a local holiday when several community partners will be unavailable. She stays quiet in the meeting and raises it with you privately afterward. Later, a senior colleague who is giving input to Maya's performance review says she "lacks leadership presence" because she didn't speak up. How do you respond?
steps.context: Contradicting a supervisor in front of the team can feel disrespectful; raising a concern privately can feel like the responsible thing to do. The distribution starts in eight days.

sources.title: UN Values and Behaviours Framework (2021)

choices.text: Fix the schedule, but agree that speaking up in meetings is part of leadership, and support noting it in her review as an area for development this year.
choices.feedback: Fixing the schedule is right, but this judges how Maya spoke, not what she said. She raised a correct concern through a channel that worked, and recording it as a weakness would penalize a communication style rather than performance.

choices.text: Tell Maya her concern was valuable, but that from now on she should raise issues in meetings, so that the whole team benefits from them.
choices.feedback: It keeps the door open, but it imposes one norm on everyone. It doesn't account for her role, the power gap with the team lead or where she feels able to speak. Widen the channels instead of narrowing them.

choices.text: Keep the schedule as presented, since partners have already seen it, and ask Maya to put her concern in writing so it can be considered for the next cycle.
choices.feedback: The clash doesn't go away because it was raised quietly or late. Treating private, correct input as less valid means partners miss the distribution, and Maya learns that raising concerns changes nothing.

choices.text: Thank Maya, fix the schedule and credit her if she wishes. Tell your colleague the concern was correct and raised responsibly, and judge input on its merits.
choices.feedback: This fixes the real problem, gives credit where it is due and answers the "presence" judgment with evidence. It widens who gets heard, which is the same "who's missing" check that Team Debrief is built for.

steps.prompt: You decide to change how input is gathered. At the next coordination meeting, a senior international colleague dominates the discussion, two national staff members start to speak and are talked over, and the only partner joining by phone from a field site can barely hear. Afterward, three people send you useful points by message. Your deputy suggests simply asking everyone to "be more assertive". What do you change?
steps.context: Meetings are held in English. Field partners join by phone on a poor connection, and the agenda is usually shared on the morning of the meeting.

sources.title: UN Values and Behaviours Framework (2021)

choices.text: Share the agenda a day ahead, open each item with a round that includes phone participants, accept written input and agree a norm against interrupting.
choices.feedback: Structure does what encouragement can't. Early agendas give people time to prepare, rounds make sure every voice is heard at least once, and written input counts contributions that arrive outside the room.

choices.text: Ask everyone to be more assertive, as your deputy suggests, and offer national staff a training session on speaking up and presenting in meetings.
choices.feedback: This puts the problem on the people being talked over rather than on how the meeting runs. Training can help individuals, but it leaves the interruptions, the timing and the phone line exactly as they are.

choices.text: Speak privately to the senior colleague about dominating the discussion, and ask them to hold back so that others, including national staff, have room to contribute.
choices.feedback: A private word can help, and it avoids embarrassing anyone, but it depends on one person changing and does nothing for the partner on a bad phone line. Combine it with changes to how the meeting runs.

choices.text: Move the meeting to a written-only format, with everyone posting updates in a shared document instead of speaking, to remove the hierarchy from the room entirely.
choices.feedback: Written input is a useful channel, but making it the only one disadvantages people less confident writing in English and removes the discussion where problems get solved together. Offer several channels, not a different single one.

steps.prompt: Three months later, you review the changes. Meetings feel calmer, but the notes show that most decisions still follow the points made by the same two senior colleagues. The written channel is used almost only by national staff, and their suggestions are summarized at the end of the notes under "other comments". A colleague says the system works because "everyone has a channel now". How do you respond?
steps.context: No one has tracked which suggestions are adopted. The field partners have stopped joining by phone.

sources.title: UN Values and Behaviours Framework (2021)

choices.text: Agree that the changes are working, since everyone now has a channel and meetings feel calmer, and plan to review the format again in six months.
choices.feedback: Having a channel isn't the same as being heard. The notes suggest written input is collected but discounted, and the partners who stopped joining are a warning sign. Calmer meetings can hide the same imbalance.

choices.text: Move the written suggestions from the end to the top of the meeting notes, so that national staff input is more visible to everyone who reads them.
choices.feedback: Visibility helps a little, but moving text up the page doesn't change whether it influences decisions, and it does nothing about the field partners who have dropped out.

choices.text: Track which suggestions are adopted and from whom, put written input on the agenda, ask field partners why they stopped joining and share the findings.
choices.feedback: Measuring whose input shapes decisions turns an impression into evidence. Treating written input as real agenda items and asking partners why they left address the imbalance itself, not just the appearance of inclusion.

choices.text: Ask the two senior colleagues to step back from decisions for a few months, so that others can take the lead and the pattern is finally broken.
choices.feedback: Breaking the pattern is the right goal, but sidelining two colleagues swaps one imbalance for another and loses their expertise. Change how decisions are made, so that every contribution is weighed, rather than who may contribute.

takeaways: Judge a concern on its merits, not on how or where it was raised.
Quiet in the meeting room is not the same as having nothing to say.
Offer several ways to give input, and check whose input actually shapes decisions.
debrief.reflection: Whose input in your team usually arrives after the meeting, and how is it counted?
